newsitem.title: USA: Lake urges CIA reward hard chargers.
newsitem.headline: Lake urges CIA reward hard chargers.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's choice for CIA director said on Wednesday he would like to reward Central Intelligence Agency personnel who tackle tough jobs even if they fail.

"Even if they fail at hard things, if they did it right and they did it honestly they need to be rewarded for it," Anthony Lake told the Senate Intelligence Committee on the second of six scheduled sessions on his nomination.
"It doesn't help us or the national interest very much when they do easy things," he added in reply to a question from Sen. Charles Robb, a Virginia Democrat.

Lake, Clinton's first-term national security adviser, applied this formula to clandestine operatives who recruit spies abroad as well as to their desk-bound colleagues "when they make tough analytical calls." He said national security would benefit if the CIA managed to learn more about countries like Iraq and Cuba.

Lake endorsed the CIA's recent purge of foreign informants judged to be outdated or whose value as tipsters was outweighed by the stigma of shady or criminal pasts. He said the worldwide "agent scrub," as it was known inside the CIA, had been completed. It took place mainly under CIA Director John Deutch, who left in December after 20 months in office.
Lake said CIA case officers now weighed the value of a source's information against the downside of any dealings "not consistent with our own values or laws."
"If they're in doubt about that balance, they refer it to Washington," where higher-ups make the call, he said. "I think this is the right way to proceed."

New CIA curbs on recruitment have triggered controversy among those who fear it may hinder U.S. ability to infiltrate terrorist cells, drug gangs and other criminal enterprises. But Lake, who has spent much of his time in recent months at CIA headquarters familiarizing himself with the job, rejected the notion that the shedding of links to the worst offenders would lead to "risk aversion" among field officers.

"In fact it makes it less likely that some young officer will be hung out to dry for having made the wrong judgment," he said. "Washington will make the judgment for them, and the responsibility appropriately lies in Washington."

Much of the hearing's anticipated political tension evaporated by the middle of the second day, strengthening the prospect that the 19-member intelligence panel will approve the nomination and send it to the full Senate, where he could still face a rough confirmation fight from Republicans.
Lake, in reply to a question from Kansas Republican Sen. Pat Roberts, complimented the tone of the proceedings set by Republican Richard Shelby of Alabama, the committee chairman.

Shelby returned for a second day to questions about Lake's management of the National Security Council staff last June, when the FBI briefed two of his aides on an alleged Chinese plan to improperly influence U.S. elections.

Lake said he should have been alerted by his aides about the FBI's concerns over any Chinese plan to steer funds secretly to candidates for federal office. "There appears to have been some kind of a breakdown here," he said of the aides' failure to pass the alert up the line to him.
But he denied it was symptomatic of any failure of his ability to manage the 151-member council staff.

If confirmed, Lake would run the CIA and serve as board chairman of its 12 companion executive branch espionage outfits, which together account for about $30 billion a year in U.S. spending and employ tens of thousands of people.
